Fine-tuning changes the behavior of a pretrained model by writing an update relative to what that model already knows. How many bits are actually required to preserve this acquired behavior? Parameter count, adapter rank, and numerical precision measure storage, but need not measure the information that matters functionally. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) provides a clean setting for studying this question: the base model remains frozen while the learned update is isolated in a separate adapter that can be compressed after training. We take a receiver-relative rate–distortion view of this process. As illustrated in Figure 1 , fine-tuning acts as an encoder, the adapter as a finite-rate message, and the frozen model as side information available when that message is decoded. We measure rate by the exact serialized size of a compressed adapter and distortion by the behavior of the resulting composed model. For a fixed retention target, the behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} is the smallest measured rate that preserves the required fraction of the held-out fine-tuning gain. This operational definition exposes a gap between numerical and behavioral compression. Lower weight reconstruction error need not preserve more learned behavior, and comparable bit budgets can have different effects depending on where compression acts. Behavioral rate also increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budget. Most importantly, the same datasets can require substantially different rates across frozen models, with their ordering changing across receivers. Compression can also reveal structure within a learned update. Under deliberately corrupted reasoning supervision, fine-tuning can strongly damage the frozen model, yet aggressive compression recovers much of the lost performance and can exceed the frozen baseline. On Qwen2.5-7B, for example, GSM8K accuracy falls from 77.6% to 23.7% after corrupted fine-tuning and returns to 82.9% after compression. Singular-direction analyses show that harmful and useful effects are distributed unevenly across the update, while matched-norm controls show that the recovery is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. Finally, once an update has been trained, its behavioral rate closely tracks how far it can be shrunk before losing its gain. A simple codec-specific rule, R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) ≈ α 90 / γ R^{\star}(0.90)\approx\alpha_{90}/\gamma , achieves an RMSE of 0.068 bits per value on 42 checkpoints from five receivers not used to fix the rule, although the evaluation remains retrospective. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning is not an intrinsic property of the data or of parameter displacement alone: it depends on the frozen receiver, the behavior to preserve, and how the learned corrections are represented within the update.

We begin by examining how post-training compression affects fine-tuned behavior. Controlled compression lets us separate numerical reconstruction from functional preservation while keeping both the learned checkpoint and the frozen model fixed. These diagnostics show that ordinary parameter-space fidelity is not sufficient to predict which compressed adapters preserve the behavior acquired during fine-tuning.

We study post-training compression of LoRA adapters across frozen language models from 0.5B to 32B parameters, including Qwen2.5-{0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B}, Qwen3-8B-Base, Mistral-7B-v0.1, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Each adapter is trained once and then compressed over a range of operating points, without retraining. At one bit per value and above, we quantize the LoRA factors row-wise; below one bit, we additionally remove paired rank directions. Each compressed representation, including its decoding metadata, is serialized to disk, reloaded, and evaluated in composition with the frozen model. We report realized file size normalized by the number of scalar values in the uncompressed adapter. Full training configurations, codec details, datasets, and evaluation procedures are given in Appendix A .

The final recovered adapter is rank 1 and one bit, raising the possibility that the same result could be obtained by training a small adapter from the start. We therefore train corrupted adapters at ranks 1, 2, 4, and 16, and compress every checkpoint to the same rank-1, one-bit endpoint. Figure 11 b shows that recovery is substantially stronger when additional rank was available during training: final GSM8K accuracy rises from approximately 60% when trained at rank 1 to approximately 78–81% when trained at ranks 2–16. Compression is therefore not equivalent to directly training the final low-rank representation. Higher training rank appears to make useful behavior more recoverable under the subsequent bottleneck, although these experiments do not establish the mechanism by which this separation emerges. Yet, how the different dynamics of the two stages manifest in the low-rank increment that LoRA optimizes remains unclear. Tracking the singular spectrum and subspaces of LoRA updates on mathematical reasoning tasks, we find that RL concentrates the spectrum at every learning rate, while SFT expands it at moderate learning rates; moreover, RL rotates the singular subspaces much faster than SFT at small learning rates. Interpolating between SFT and RL one ingredient at a time, we pinpoint group-mean baseline subtraction as the source of both contrasts. A quadratic multi-index model updated via LoRA unveils the underlying mechanism: group-mean baseline subtraction tilts the balance between two competing forces, coherent fitting and gradient noise, toward spectral concentration and faster subspace rotation, while forcing the risk-favorable learning rate to be low. Guided by these dynamics, we tailor LoRA updates to each stage: in SFT, we flatten the spectrum of the full update to spread adaptation across singular directions, whereas in RL, we flatten the part of the update outside the current LoRA increment span to promote subspace rotation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning tasks across multiple models show that the respective configurations for SFT and RL yield the best performance among the compared methods in most evaluated settings.

passages.text: Muon has recently emerged as a promising optimizer for pretraining large language models, offering a speedup over AdamW in minimizing pretraining loss. However, it remains unclear whether Muon’s advantage persists after fine-tuning. In this paper, we study the downstream behavior of Muon and AdamW and uncover a surprising trend: beyond a sufficiently large pretraining data budget, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning. Moreover, as model size increases, AdamW overtakes Muon at progressively smaller pretraining token–parameter ratios. To explain this reversal, we view fine-tuning as a perturbation of the outputs and introduce the margin-to-spread ratio, which measures how far the correct logit lies above the wrong ones relative to how widely the wrong logits are spread. In language models, Muon has the larger margin-to-spread ratio at small data budgets and AdamW at large ones, mirroring the fine-tuning trend. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the margin-to-spread ratio of gradient descent gains on that of Muon as the data budget grows, and simulations show that this trend persists after extended training. Catherine Li ∗ Jingchu Gai ∗ Andrej Risteski Jacob Mitchell Springer † Aditi Raghunathan † Carnegie Mellon University {catheri4, jgai}@andrew.cmu.edu

The Muon optimizer has recently shown strong empirical performance for pretraining LLMs, challenging AdamW’s status as the standard optimizer for minimizing pretraining loss ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) . Prior work has shown that the pretraining optimization choices that minimize pretraining loss do not necessarily yield the best model after fine-tuning ( Watts et al., 2026 ) . What ultimately matters downstream is the learning–forgetting tradeoff : how well a fine-tuned model learns the target task while retaining its pretrained knowledge. Motivated by this, we ask: Does Muon’s pretraining advantage over AdamW extend to the learning–forgetting tradeoff? To answer this question, we measure the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap , which compares the two optimizers on this tradeoff; a negative gap indicates that the Muon pretrained model dominates the AdamW pretrained model after fine-tuning, and a positive gap indicates the reverse. We show that the answer depends on the pretraining data budget, and find that pretraining data scale reverses the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap . At small budgets, Muon achieves lower fine-tuning loss with less forgetting than AdamW and the fine-tuning gap is negative. At larger budgets, this trend reverses: AdamW achieves a better learning–forgetting tradeoff than Muon, and the fine-tuning gap becomes positive.

In Section 3 , we pretrain OLMo-style 30M–600M models ( Groeneveld et al., 2024 ; Team OLMo et al., 2025 ) on 150 150 M to 154 154 B DCLM tokens ( Li et al., 2024 ) , comparing AdamW and Muon, and fine-tune each base model on four datasets while sweeping the fine-tuning optimizer and learning rate, for nearly 600 pretraining runs and 29,000 fine-tuning runs in total. We show that when tuning pretraining hyperparameters for the lowest pretraining loss, Muon consistently achieves lower loss than AdamW. However, with sufficient pretraining data, AdamW outperforms Muon after fine-tuning, reversing the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap. This reversal also holds when we disregard pretraining loss, instead sweeping pretraining hyperparameters to obtain the best learning–forgetting tradeoff after fine-tuning. We additionally show that as model size scales, AdamW surpasses Muon at progressively smaller data budgets . In Section 4 , we investigate why the Muon–AdamW fine-tuning gap reverses as the pretraining data budget grows. Fine-tuning changes the output distribution, so we generalize fine-tuning updates with perturbations to the output distribution and study which optimizer produces base models that are more robust to such perturbations. To quantify sensitivity to output perturbations, we introduce the margin-to-spread ratio (MSR) , a simple metric derived from the model’s output logits that characterizes robustness. For each prediction, the MSR is the difference between the correct logit and the average of the incorrect logits, normalized by the spread of the incorrect logits ( Section 4.1 ): a prediction is more robust when the MSR is larger.

We test whether the budget trend predicted by Section 4.2 also appears in real language models, beyond the assumptions used in our theoretical analysis. Setup. We evaluate the AdamW and Muon models trained in Section 3 , spanning five model sizes, on held-out DCLM text. We compute the MSR at each token position and report the median over correctly predicted positions. At each position, h h and κ \kappa are the mean and standard deviation of the margins between the correct next-token logit and all other vocabulary logits. We use the median to reduce sensitivity to outliers; Section 4.1 instead uses the mean margin divided by the square root of the mean variance. Experimental Result. Figure 5 plots the MSR for the three model sizes with the widest budget ranges, from 30M to 100M. Muon has a larger MSR at small data budgets, while AdamW has a larger MSR at sufficiently large budgets. As the budget grows, the difference between AdamW’s and Muon’s MSRs increases, and the ratio of AdamW’s MSR to Muon’s crosses one. This shift toward AdamW is consistent with the theoretical budget trend and parallels the reversal in relative robustness to fine-tuning observed in Section 3 . Figure 5: In real language models, the margin-to-spread ratio of AdamW gains on Muon’s as the token budget grows. (a) MSR ρ \rho of AdamW and Muon against pretraining TPR for 30M, 60M, and 100M models: Muon has the larger MSR at small budgets and AdamW at large ones. (b) The MSR ratio ρ AdamW / ρ Muon \rho^{\mathrm{AdamW}}/\rho^{\mathrm{Muon}} crosses one as the budget grows, at every model size.

The MSR and fine-tuning crossovers do not necessarily appear at exactly the same budget, since the learning–forgetting tradeoff also depends on pretraining loss. Nevertheless, the MSR captures the direction of the observed shift and connects our theoretical analysis to the behavior of trained language models. Remark. We summarize the analysis of this section and relate MSR to other metrics used to predict post-training. • Takeaway. In a linear associative memory, we prove that after one update the ratio ρ GD / ρ Muon \rho^{\mathrm{GD}}/\rho^{\mathrm{Muon}} of the two optimizers’ MSRs increases with the data budget ( Section 4.2 ). Simulations of many training steps show that the same trend persists after extended training ( Section 4.2 ). • Extension: Relation of MSR to Other Metrics Predicting Post-Training. Other work predicts forgetting after post-training with different metrics. For example, Springer et al. (2025) show that the loss increase after adding Gaussian noise to the pretrained weights tracks how much a model degrades under fine-tuning. In Appendix B , we show that MSR is connected to this robustness to Gaussian perturbations: in the linear memory, a larger MSR provably guarantees that more competitors stay ranked below the correct answer after the perturbation ( Section B.2.1 ), and in both language models and the linear memory, MSR is strongly correlated with perturbation robustness ( Section B.2.2 ).

Figures 11 and 10 extend the frontiers and gaps of the lowest-pretraining-loss setting ( Figures 1 and 3 ) to all four datasets, at the budgets around each crossover. passages.text: Matrix factorization provides a simple model for studying the training dynamics of neural networks. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton–Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). We show that the number of Newton–Schulz steps can change the rank selected during the early stages of training and allow the resulting trajectory to bypass the first nonzero stationary point approached by gradient flow. Under an additional residual-inertia condition, we prove that bypass occurs for all sufficiently large finite Newton–Schulz depths and provide an explicit sufficient threshold. We also construct an example in which the bypass threshold is four. † † shortheadings: Finite-Depth Newton–Schulz Dynamics / Long † † firstpage: 1 † † heading: 2026 1–

We consider a two-layer neural network with quadratic activation and all second-layer weights fixed to one. This model admits an equivalent representation as a positive-semidefinite matrix factorization. Such quadratic networks provide a tractable setting for analyzing nonlinear training dynamics, and have also been studied through gradient flow and spectral gradient methods ( Martin et al., 2024 ; Martin et al., 2026 ; Braun et al., 2026 ) . passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

CORE achieves the highest answer accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark group, producing new state-of-the-art results. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves both metrics over the stronger baseline, OpenResearcher, for all three agent models. The gains are largest for Qwen3.8-27B, at 6.39 points in accuracy and 7.40 points in recall. On BrowseComp-Wikipedia, CORE keeps its lead across all three agents. With GPT-5.4, it improves both metrics by more than eight points over OpenResearcher. Higher accuracy therefore comes with broader coverage of the annotated relevant documents in both the web and Wikipedia corpora. See some case studies in Appendix C .

With Qwen3.8-27B, Tongyi DeepResearch is the stronger baseline in accuracy, and CORE still exceeds both baselines in accuracy and recall.

Existing low-rank ZO methods either parameterize the additive update through Euclidean factors with a non-unique representation, or restrict each finite-difference direction to be low-rank. In this work, we propose to constrain each additive update block to a fixed-rank matrix manifold while keeping the pretrained weights frozen, so the learned update remains rank-constrained throughout fine-tuning. On this geometry, we build a Riemannian ZO gradient estimator that projects a random matrix onto the tangent space, normalizes it to correct the scale mismatch induced by projection, and further propose Zeroth-order Riemannian Gradient Descent (ZO-RGD) and its smoothed variant, ZO-RGD-S. We show that the ambient finite difference matches its retracted counterpart, the normalized estimator recovers the Riemannian gradient in expectation, and ZO-RGD converges under trajectory-regularity conditions. Experiments on LLM fine-tuning tasks show that the proposed algorithms are competitive with strong forward-only baselines across model families and tasks, with gains in several settings.

passages.text: The rapid scaling of large language models (LLMs) has made communication overhead a critical bottleneck in distributed model-parallel training. Although existing low-precision compression methods can effectively reduce communication costs, further reducing the communication footprint to ultra-low-bit formats such as FP4 introduces new challenges, including limited numerical range, sub-byte storage overhead, and increased computational cost from fine-grained quantization. In this paper, we present FP4Quant , a micro-grouped FP4 compression framework for efficient model-parallel LLM training. FP4Quant integrates a micro-grouped dual-scale FP4 quantization mechanism to preserve local tensor distribution characteristics, a warp-cooperative FP4 packing scheme to enable efficient sub-byte data representation, and a hybrid two-level FWHT pipeline to mitigate quantization errors with GPU-aware execution optimization. Experiments on NVIDIA H100 GPUs with Qwen-7B demonstrate up to 1.56 × \times end-to-end throughput improvement over BF16, revealing a trade-off between throughput and model quality.

We train Qwen-7B on the OpenWebMath corpus. Model quality is evaluated using validation loss and the corresponding perplexity (PPL) ( PPL = e loss \mathrm{PPL}=e^{\text{loss}} ). System efficiency is measured by end-to-end training throughput (TFLOP/s per GPU) under different parallel settings. Downstream model capability is further evaluated using accuracy on CMMLU and C-Eval .

We evaluate FP4Quant under three parallel regimes: TP, PP, and their combined MP configuration in large-scale distributed training. For each regime, we investigate micro-group sizes G ∈ 64,128,256,512 G\in{64,128,256,512} and compare against two baselines: the uncompressed BF16 (Ring) and Tahquant , a representative method for activation communication compression in PP settings. Training loss and downstream accuracy reflect different aspects of model performance: loss measures optimization convergence, whereas downstream tasks evaluate practical model capability. Although the two metrics are not strictly correlated, poor convergence or substantially higher loss than the baseline typically leads to degraded downstream performance. Table 1 reports evaluation results on CMMLU and C-Eval (valid) with G = 64 G=64 . FP4Quant consistently preserves downstream performance across model-parallel settings, achieving scores of 0.5287 / 0.4829 0.5287/0.4829 (TP), 0.5288 / 0.5342 0.5288/0.5342 (PP), and 0.5301 / 0.5253 0.5301/0.5253 (MP), compared with the BF16 baseline ( 0.5365 / 0.5215 0.5365/0.5215 ). Notably, under PP and MP configurations, FP4Quant matches or slightly exceeds BF16 on C-Eval, demonstrating strong capability preservation under ultra-low-bit compression. In contrast, TahQuant exhibits severe degradation under communication-intensive settings. Under TP and MP, its performance drops to near random-chance levels ( 0.2530 / 0.2771 0.2530/0.2771 and 0.2534 / 0.2422 0.2534/0.2422 ), while remaining stable only under PP. This suggests that coarse-grained 4-bit quantization is insufficient to maintain optimization quality, ultimately degrading downstream performance. Overall, FP4Quant achieves both consistently stable convergence and superior downstream fidelity compared with existing 4-bit communication methods. Table 2: Comparison of training accuracy and throughput between FP4Quant and baselines (BF16 and Tahquant) under TP4 and PP on Qwen-7B.

Table 2 shows that FP4Quant achieves a superior balance between training accuracy and throughput compared to BF16. Under TP, Tahquant attains the highest throughput (197.4 TFLOP/s/GPU, 1.78 × 1.78\times ), but suffers from severe accuracy degradation, indicating that its aggressive quantization compromises training fidelity. In contrast, FP4Quant substantially improves model quality while still providing significant speedup. At G = 64 G=64 , FP4Quant reduces the loss to 2.2306 while achieving a 1.40 × 1.40\times speedup over BF16, and continues to offer a favorable trade-off at larger group sizes. For example, at G = 256 G=256 , FP4Quant reaches 173.3 TFLOP/s/GPU while achieving significantly better accuracy than Tahquant. Although FP4Quant achieves lower throughput than Tahquant, it avoids severe accuracy degradation while delivering a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off. Under PP, where computation dominates execution and communication overhead is less significant, all methods achieve comparable throughput (189–191 TFLOP/s/GPU). FP4Quant reaches 190.1–191.1 TFLOP/s/GPU, closely matching the BF16 baseline (189.1 TFLOP/s/GPU) with up to 1.01 × 1.01\times speedup, indicating that its quantization and scaling overhead is effectively hidden by computation. Unlike communication-bound TP training, PP offers limited acceleration potential because performance is primarily determined by computation throughput. Overall, FP4Quant enables efficient low-bit communication with substantial acceleration under TP while incurring negligible runtime overhead under PP, demonstrating its effectiveness across diverse parallel configurations.
